I don't think that fans consider themselves actually part of the team (unless they're outright delusional), but sports by nature is a collectivistic pursuit. When you support a team you immediately given positive social feedback from fellow supporters and negative feedback from opposing ones, entrenching what would otherwise be a very superficial and self-made false dichotomy. But we personalize our experience with these teams because it intensifies the feelings that go along with supporting those teams, and offers us greater opportunities for this positive social feedback.

I also think language plays a role in that the "we" becomes a collectivistic "we" as just shorthand for "our team". By contrast, look at individual sports - have you ever heard anyone say "My Floyd Mayweather" or "Our Serena Williams"? I think the only exception here would be international competitions like the Olympics where individuals represent "our" country.

Most people know that sports are a just a pastime and prefer to bask in the benefits of the in-group mentality rather than acting on this arbitrary US/THEM belief system against the out-group in a way that will get them in trouble; however, you only need to look at all of the hooliganism in sports to see what that kind of black and white thinking will appear to justify in a person's mind, and how dangerous that thinking could be to much more important areas such as religion and politics.

The Supremacy Clause (Article 6, Clause 2) states:

The supremacy of federal law over state law only applies if Congress is acting in pursuance of its constitutionally authorized powers.

Congress's authorized powers, according to Article 1, Section 8 of the Constitution:

The Congress shall have power * To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common defence[note 1] and general Welfare of the United States; but all Duties, Imposts and Excises shall be uniform throughout the United States;

A General Welfare clause is defined as:

A general welfare clause is a section that appeared in many constitutions, as well as in some charters and statutes, which provides that the governing body empowered by the document may enact laws to promote the general welfare of the people, sometimes worded as the public welfare. In some countries, this has been used as a basis for legislation promoting the health, safety, morals, and well-being of the people governed thereunder (known as the police power). Such clauses are generally interpreted as granting the state broad power to legislate or regulate for the general welfare that is independent of other powers specified in the governing document.

That is a an overview, but specific to the US Constitution, the General Welfare clause allows Congress to spend the collected money "on matters of general interest to the federal government". And one of their general interests is "providing individuals with comprehensive family planning and related preventive health services," aka Title X, which is how Planned Parenthood gets paid. So it's totally within the power of the federal government to be responsible for with existing tax money.
